Atlantic spadefish (Chaetodipterus faber) are iteroparous, broadcast-spawning reef fish that exhibit a relatively rapid early life history when maintained at a water temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion following an incubation period of six days [ab = six days], a duration that is consistent with the embryonic development rates reported for other ephippid species at similar temperatur at a temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]es. The newly emerged larva is initially endotrophic, relying entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. This brief embryonic phase and small initial size reflect the energetic constraints of producing many small, buoyant pelagic eggs, a reproductive strategy common among tropical and subtropical marine teleosts. The larval period is characterised by rapid morphological changes, including the development of the mouth gape and the inflation of the swim bladder, both of which are critical for the transition to active predation in the planktonic environment.

The maximum total length achieved by adult Atlantic spadefish has been recorded at 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of the family Ephippidae. This ultimate size is attained through a prolonged period of somatic growth that continues well after the onset of sexual maturation. In comparison with congeneric species such as Chaetodipterus zonatus, the spadefish exhibits a moderately robust body form that is laterally compressed, an adaptation that facilitates manoeuvrability within structurally complex reef habitats. Field surveys and tag-recapture studies indicate that individuals approach this asymptotic length gradually, with most annual growth increments becoming substantially reduced after the fish have reached approximately 60 to 70 percent of their maximum length. The species is known to form large, slow-moving aggregations over sandy flats and around artificial reef structures, where they are frequently observed by recreational divers.

Sexual maturation in Atlantic spadefish occurs at a relatively modest body size, with individuals becoming reproductively active once they attain a total length of approximately 14 centimeters [Lp = approximately 14 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet body mass of roughly 33.1 grams [Wwp = roughly 33.1 grams], a mass that is far smaller than the ultimate adult weight and indicates that the species allocates resources to reproductive effort early in its life history. Histological examination of gonadal tissue reveals that both ovaries and testes begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis, respectively, near this size threshold. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 7% [GSI = 7%] in gravid females collected during the spawning season at 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]. This value is consistent with an iteroparous, multiple-batch spawning strategy.

The wet weight of a newly hatched Atlantic spadefish larva is approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the pelagic egg, which averages about one millimeter. This exceedingly small neonatal mass is typical of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, planktonic offspring. At the other extreme, the species attains a considerable ultimate wet weight, with the largest documented individuals reaching as much as 9,100 grams [Wwi = 9,100 grams] in total body mass. The enormous disparity between the hatchling mass and the ultimate adult mass—spanning several orders of magnitude—underscores the intensive feeding and rapid growth that occur during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, particularly once the fish transition from a planktivorous larval diet to a benthic omnivorous diet that includes small crustaceans, polychaetes, and algae.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Atlantic spadefish under natural conditions is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], based on otolith age estimates from populations inhabiting coastal waters of the southeastern United States at a mean annual water temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]. This longevity is moderate compared to other members of the Ephippidae, reflecting a life history strategy that balances early reproduction with sustained somatic growth over an extended adult phase. The species attains sexual maturity at a relatively small fraction of its maximum age and size, a pattern that confers resilience to moderate levels of fishing pressure. However, the relatively late age at which individuals reach the full adult body size suggests that the population may be vulnerable to size-selective harvest, particularly of the larger, more fecund individuals. Continued monitoring of age structure and reproductive output is essential for the long-term management of this species.
